usage: the bound pre-counter form of 스물; the only native ten that shrinks
스물 → 스무 before 살, the most common use
개 counts objects; never 스물 개
명 counts people; the ㄹ of 스물 still drops
examples: age + 살; 스물 contracts to 스무
the counter 개 forces 스무, not 스물 개

nuance: 스무 is the bound, pre-counter shape of 스물 (twenty) — it drops the final ㄹ exactly the way 하나→한, 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네 lose or change their ending before a counter. The headline fact: among the native TENS, 스물 is the sole survivor of this contraction — 서른·마흔·쉰·예순·일흔·여든·아흔 all keep their full shape (서른 살, 마흔 개), so '스무' is special and not a pattern to over-apply. Use it before any counter (스무 살, 스무 개, 스무 명, 스무 시간), but the instant no counter follows you snap back to 스물 ('스물이 넘어요', counting '…열아홉, 스물'). The twin English-speaker errors are forgetting to contract ('스물 살') and over-contracting the higher tens (there is no '서르 살').

usage: interrogative quantifier; sits in a number's slot before a counter
개 counts objects; 몇 + 개 asks a quantity
literally 'how many o'clock'; the hour uses native counting
examples: 몇 시 is the standard way to ask the hour
How many people are in your family?
몇 + 명 asks number of people
Just give me a few apples.
nuance: 몇 means 'how many' and, grammatically, behaves like a number: it drops straight into the slot before a counter (몇 개, 몇 명, 몇 시, 몇 잔), and since it pairs with the native-number counters, it inherits their world (몇 시 'what time', 몇 살 'how old'). A defining subtlety is that the SAME 몇 also means 'a few / several' when it is not a question — '몇 개 샀어요' can be 'I bought a few' depending on intonation and context. Two boundaries trip English speakers: (1) 몇 almost always needs a counter, so 'how many?' about countable things is 몇 개/몇 명, not bare 몇; (2) don't confuse 몇 시 (what TIME, native + 시) with 며칠 (what DATE/how many days, which behaves on the Sino-Korean date system) — different question, different number family. Compare also 얼마나 'how much/to what extent', which asks degree rather than a countable number.

usage: native ordinal for #1; also 'first of all' when listing
the eldest child; 첫째 alone can mean 'the eldest'
first day of a trip, course, or job
the next native ordinal, used in the same series as 첫째
examples: 첫째 alone names birth order in a family
On the first day of the trip we went to the sea.
첫째 날 = the first day in a sequence
First of all, health matters most.
첫째 opens a list, pairing with 둘째 next
nuance: 첫째 is the native-Korean ordinal 'first', built from 첫 (the bound 'first' form of 하나) + the ordinal suffix -째; the rest of the family runs 둘째, 셋째, 넷째 'second/third/fourth'. It does three jobs: it names the eldest child (저는 첫째예요), it labels the first item in a sequence (첫째 날, 첫째 주 'first week'), and it works like 'firstly/first of all' to organize spoken or written points, almost always followed by 둘째. Don't confuse the ORDINAL system (첫째, 둘째 — order/rank) with the CARDINAL-plus-번/번째 way of listing (일 번, 1번째 'item no. 1'); 첫째 ranks, 일 번 labels. Also note the bound adjective 첫 'first' (첫사랑 first love, 첫날 first day, 첫인상 first impression) — same root, but 첫 attaches to a noun while 첫째 stands as the ordinal itself. A common slip is using the plain number 하나 to mean 'first'; ordering requires 첫째, never 하나.
